title: Website Maintenance Guide
text:
cd ~/Documents/Playground/website

# 1. Edit any .qmd file (add a paper, update teaching, etc.)

# 2. Preview locally to check it looks right:
~/opt/quarto/bin/quarto preview

# 3. When happy, publish to the live site:
~/opt/quarto/bin/quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt
Step 2 starts a local server (usually at http://localhost:4567) that auto-reloads when you save a file — so you can edit and see changes in real time.
Step 3 re-renders everything, pushes the built HTML to the gh-pages branch on GitHub, and your live site updates within ~1 minute.


The publish command only pushes the rendered site. To save your source files (the .qmd files you actually edit), commit and push to main separately:
git add -A
git commit -m "description of what you changed"
git push
This is good practice so your source files are backed up and versioned. You don’t have to do this every time you publish, but do it regularly.





Preview before publishing. Always run quarto preview and check the site in your browser before running quarto publish. Catches typos, broken links, and layout issues before they go live.
Keep source files on main. The gh-pages branch is managed automatically by quarto publish — never edit it directly. Your edits go in the .qmd files on main.
Commit often. After any meaningful edit session, commit your .qmd changes to main and push. This gives you version history (easy to undo mistakes) and a backup on GitHub.
One thing at a time. When updating, make one change, preview it, then move on. Easier to catch issues than batching many edits.
Update your CV PDF when you update the CV page. The CV page (cv.qmd) is a summary — the linked PDF (files/cv-sharon.pdf) is the full version. Keep them in sync. After recompiling your LaTeX CV, copy the new PDF into files/.
Check on mobile. After publishing, pull up your site on your phone once in a while. The CSS is responsive, but it’s good to verify.





Don’t edit files in _site/. That folder is auto-generated by quarto render. Any changes there will be overwritten next time you render. Always edit the .qmd source files.
Don’t edit the gh-pages branch. Same idea — it’s managed by quarto publish.
Don’t commit _site/ or .quarto/ to main. These are in .gitignore for a reason. They’re build artifacts, not source files.
Don’t put sensitive info on the site. No home address, personal phone number, or private links. Your email and office are fine.
Don’t let it go stale. An out-of-date website is worse than no website. When you publish a paper, give a talk, or change roles, update the site. A quick “last updated” check every quarter is a good habit.







File
What it does




_quarto.yml
Site config: title, navbar links, theme


styles.css
All custom styling (colors, fonts, layout)


index.qmd
Home page (bio, photo, interests, news)


research.qmd
Research descriptions


publications.qmd
Papers and talks


teaching.qmd
Teaching experience


cv.qmd
CV summary + link to PDF


diversions.qmd
Non-academic stuff


images/
Your photo and any future images


files/
CV PDF and any future downloadable files


_site/
Auto-generated output (don’t edit)


.gitignore
Tells git to skip _site/, .quarto/, .DS_Store








Edit publications.qmd and add a block:
::: {.pub-entry}
**Zhou, S.** et al. (2027). Your new paper title. [*Journal Name*]{.pub-venue}
[doi](https://doi.org/...){.pub-links} [pdf](files/your-paper.pdf){.pub-links}
:::



Same file, under the Talks section — same format but without the link badges.



Edit index.qmd and add a line at the top of the News list:
- **Fall 2026** — Description of the news item



Replace images/main-photo.jpg with your new photo (same filename), then publish.



In styles.css, find the :root block near the top and change --accent:
--accent: #2b6777;  /* teal — change this hex code */




Create a new .qmd file (e.g., software.qmd)
Add it to the navbar in _quarto.yml under left:
Preview and publish

title: Sharon Zhou
text:
PhD Student · Committee on Evolutionary Biology · University of Chicago
I study a problem that recurs across evolutionary biology: telling whether selection acts on a trait itself, or on something correlated with it. In genomes that “something” is genetic linkage; across the tree of life it is ecology, geography, and shared ancestry. I work the question in two systems - the population genetics of linked stabilizing selection, and the macroevolution of morphological complexity in marine bivalves - building models that ask when the true target of selection can be identified.
I’m a PhD student in Evolutionary Biology at the University of Chicago, working with David Jablonski on macroevolution and morphological complexity, and with Jeremy Berg on population-genetic theory and linked selection.

Email · Google Scholar · GitHub

title: Teaching
text:
Teaching Assistant, Quantitative Genetics for the 21st Century
Spring 2026
Supported a mixed undergraduate/graduate cohort in bridging quantitative genetic theory — including the Breeder’s equation, causal inference, and GWAS — with hands-on R implementation through weekly office hours and coding assignments. Also moderated in-class paper discussions on the intersections of race, ancestry, and complex traits, with attention to scientific rigor and respectful academic discourse.


Teaching Assistant, Biological Evolution
Winter 2026
Facilitated active-learning discussion sections for non-majors and majors, guiding students through primary literature analysis and evolutionary theory. Co-developed inquiry-based curriculum for a Field Museum experiential learning module, helping students synthesize morphological data with evolutionary hypotheses.

title: Research
text:
My research asks how complex phenotypes become unevenly distributed across the tree of life, geography, and time. I combine fossil data, comparative biology, population-genetic theory, and computational modeling to distinguish direct selection on traits from indirect sorting through correlated ecological, geographic, and genetic factors.
These two programs look nothing alike as systems, but they are the same inferential problem at different scales: an observed signal of selection may identify the trait selection actually targeted, or a correlated neighbor - a linked locus in a genome, a covarying ecological or geographic trait across lineages - and the work is to tell which, and to know when the data can.

title: Research
text:
Morphological complexity and macroevolution
I study the origination and differential sorting of morphological complexity in marine bivalves. My work has shown that functional disparity in bivalves did not follow an “early burst” pattern despite rapid taxonomic diversification in the early Paleozoic; rather, taxonomy, morphology, and ecology followed distinct evolutionary trajectories, demonstrating that biodiversity currencies are not interchangeable.
My current thesis work investigates why phenotypic complexity is unevenly distributed across latitude, clades, and the fossil record. Using a feature-explicit complexity score for bivalve ornamentation, we found that species richness and ornamentation complexity decouple across latitude, driven mainly by sorting among families with conserved complexity baselines rather than by within-family transformation. This raises questions about the historical assembly and persistence of lineage-level complexity regimes, and when apparent morphological selectivity reflects direct selection on phenotypes versus indirect sorting through correlated traits such as ecology, geographic range, life history, among others.
Advisor: David Jablonski

title: Research
section: Impact of linked stabilizing selection on genetic diversity
text:
Impact of linked stabilizing selection on genetic diversity
We developed a moments model for the impact of stabilizing selection on linked genomic diversity. Classical background-selection theory assumes directional purifying selection, but stabilizing selection - thought to shape much of human complex-trait variation - defines a distinct and underexplored regime. Our model, validated against forward simulations, shows that stabilizing selection produces a greater reduction in linked neutral diversity than the classical additive purifying-selection prediction; we are now working out why, using population-genetic theory.
Work with: Jeremy Berg
